QF.id: SIA Case Studies on SAS Standards_46

question.text: The SE planted 10,000 mangrove seedlings. Under SAS-500, why are MANGROVE plantations given a higher SROI coefficient than upland plantations?

answer.text: Mangroves combine carbon sequestration + storm-surge / coastal protection + fisheries nursery + high per-hectare biomass — so the monetised ecosystem service per hectare is higher (blue-carbon economics)

explanation.text: The Logic: Mangrove ('blue carbon') ecosystems provide stacked ecosystem services — carbon sequestration, storm-surge and coastal protection, fisheries-nursery function, and high per-hectare biomass. Because the monetised value of these stacked services per hectare is higher than for upland plantations, ecosystem-service valuation produces a higher SROI coefficient for mangrove planting. The Trap: Options B, C and D ('cheaper', 'look nicer', 'grow faster') are trivial reasons that do not relate to ecosystem-service valuation and do not drive an SROI coefficient. Note: The specific mangrove, blue-carbon, storm-surge protection, fisheries-nursery and higher-SROI-coefficient discussion is not described in the cited Social Impact Assessors Certification Examination Workbook (January 2026) pages 43, 117 or 164-168, which cover SAS-500 environmental sustainability metrics such as green cover, biodiversity, soil/water quality, groundwater and watershed management. The framing above reflects general blue-carbon and ecosystem-service-valuation knowledge.
